one_liner: Embedded typed-key B+tree store (formerly hamsterdb) whose in-engine aggregates beat cursor scans in LevelDB and Berkeley DB.
what_it_does: upscaledb is an embedded key-value engine with a C API (ups_env_*, ups_db_*, ups_cursor_*) and C++, Java, .NET, Python and Erlang wrappers. It stores sorted keys in a B+tree and offers transactions, journalling and recovery, duplicate keys, record-number databases, AES encryption, CRC32 checks, key and record compression, and remote access over TCP. Keys and records can be declared as typed PODs (uint32, uint64, real32 and others). A small SQL-like query interface, UQI (uqi_select('MAX($record) FROM DATABASE 1'), plus COUNT, SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, TOP, BOTTOM and user-written predicate or aggregate plugins), runs full or ranged scans inside the engine. It is not API-compatible with LevelDB or Berkeley DB.
how_it_is_fast: For fixed-size typed keys and records it uses a PAX-style leaf layout (btree_impl_pax.h): a page holds a dense key array and a separate record array, which gives tight, cache-friendly loops. Lookups inside a node run a binary search that switches to an SSE2 linear search once the remaining range is small (simd.h). uint32 keys can be compressed with integer codecs such as VarByte/MaskedVByte, SIMDComp, FOR and SIMD-FOR (the Lemire and Rupp work), and files are memory-mapped by default. The headline gain comes from UQI: btree_visit.cc walks the leaf chain and hands each leaf's key and record arrays to a scan visitor (the MAX visitor is a plain scalar loop), with no per-record cursor call or key/record copy. The baselines instead iterate 50 million records one at a time through their client APIs.
when_to_use: Embedded stores keyed by integers (uint32/uint64 ids, timestamps) with small fixed-size records, where you want MIN/MAX/SUM/COUNT/AVERAGE or a custom aggregate over all or a key range of the data without writing an iteration loop
Read-mostly or append-ordered workloads on one node, where a B+tree with typed, compressed integer keys keeps the index small
Applications that need transactions, journalling and duplicate keys in one embeddable library under Apache-2.0, and that can fork and maintain it
Research or teaching on PAX layouts, SIMD in-node search and integer-key compression inside a real B+tree
when_not_to_use: New production systems that need a maintained dependency: the last commit is 2021-08-20, builds fail with current Boost.Asio and protobuf (issues #134 and #135, no maintainer reply), and issue #134 links a Homebrew-core commit titled 'upscaledb: deprecate'
Write-heavy random-insert workloads at scale: a 2014 comparison by the same author (search snippets only) found it slower than LevelDB on random writes past about 10 million keys
Multi-threaded write throughput: every public API call takes the environment's mutex, so operations on one environment are serialised

Workloads where you need cursor correctness under transactions to be proven: open issues report cursors skipping entries (#106), moving the wrong way (#107), finding erased items with UPS_FIND_GEQ_MATCH (#105) and endless recursion in cursor find (#50), and three unit tests failing (#111)
Choosing it on the 90x/140x claim alone: that measures an in-engine aggregate against client-side iteration, not general key-value speed

integration.dependencies: Boost >= 1.53 (system, filesystem, thread, chrono), protobuf (remote access), OpenSSL for AES (optional), zlib/snappy/lzf for compression, tcmalloc (optional), libdb-dev only for its comparison tests; autotools build (./configure && make) or an MSVC 2013 solution; shared and static libraries are both built.
integration.min_toolchain: C++0x/C++11 (configure forces -std=c++0x); last fixes target GCC 10.2 and MSVC 2013; newer Boost.Asio (strand template change) and protobuf break the build
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, other Unix, Windows (MSVC 2013, MinGW); x86 builds use SSE2/SSE4 when /proc/cpuinfo shows them, with a non-SIMD fallback added in 2018
integration.thread_safety: Each public API function locks the environment mutex (ScopedLock lock(env->mutex) in upscaledb.cc), so handles may be shared across threads but calls are serialised. The key->data and record->data pointers returned by lookups are not thread-safe unless you use UPS_KEY_USER_ALLOC/UPS_RECORD_USER_ALLOC (upscaledb.h). UQI plugins must be stateless.

gotchas: A plain ./configure && make builds without optimisation. configure.ac sets CFLAGS to '-DNDEBUG' before AC_PROG_CC, which suppresses autoconf's default -O2, and then overwrites CXXFLAGS with "$CFLAGS -std=c++0x", so any CXXFLAGS you set are discarded. Pass CFLAGS='-O2 -DNDEBUG' (the RPM spec passes RPM_OPT_FLAGS).

Harness flaw: the homepage labels the run 'upscaledb v2.0.0', but no such release exists (hamsterdb 2.0.0 shipped in January 2012 with no analytical functions; the hola API arrived in May 2014). The published driver calls uqi_select with typed records, which the ChangeLog dates to 2016-02-23 (upscaledb 2.2.0). The label and the code do not match, and the driver's MAX check only prints a message on a wrong result (its exit is commented out).

Licensing changed over time: hamsterdb was GPL, upscaledb 2.1.12-2.2.0 were GPL-3.0 (ChangeLog, Sep 2015), and only 2.2.1/master are Apache-2.0. Take the code from master or 2.2.1, not older tarballs.

The default cache is about 2 MB (UPS_DEFAULT_CACHE_SIZE) and files are memory-mapped by default (UPS_DISABLE_MMAP turns this off). Size the cache with UPS_PARAM_CACHE_SIZE before comparing it with other engines.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against LMDB, the closest catalogued B+tree sibling, pick upscaledb only when you need typed, compressed integer keys and built-in aggregates (MIN/MAX/SUM/COUNT/TOP over a key range) and are prepared to maintain an abandoned codebase; otherwise LMDB is the safer B+tree choice. LevelDB, the RocksDB derivatives, Badger and the other LSM siblings suit write-heavy random inserts better.
verified_claims_summary: The first-party homepage (seen only as a search snippet) says a full scan of 50 million uint32 key/record pairs to find the maximum record, with 4 MB of cache on 64-bit Linux, ran about 90x faster than LevelDB 1.11.0 and 140x faster than Berkeley DB 5.1.0. No absolute times, CPU or library build flags are given. The linked gist shows that upscaledb computed MAX inside the engine over PAX leaf arrays, while LevelDB (compression off) and Berkeley DB walked every record through an iterator or cursor in a driver compiled with g++ -std=c++11 -g -O0, one run each. The comparison therefore measures pushing an aggregate into the engine against client-side iteration, and the run is labelled with a version older than the API it uses.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit is 2021-08-20 (an MSVC 2013 build fix), the newest open issues are unanswered build failures with current Boost and protobuf, and a Homebrew-core 'deprecate' commit is linked from issue #134. It is Apache-2.0 from 2.2.1, so it is copyable, but expect to patch the build and to own the open cursor-correctness issues.
